newsitem.title: SPAIN: Union proposal could get Spain labour talks moving.
newsitem.headline: Union proposal could get Spain labour talks moving.

text.p: A move by one of Spain's two biggest unions on Thursday towards more flexible terms for dismissing workers seemed to signal tentative progress in sluggish labour reform talks with employers.
The Workers' Commissions (CCOO) union said it was putting the finishing touches to a proposal to allow companies' profitability to be considered among the criteria for fair causes for firing staff.
But the criteria include the proviso that employers should only opt for dismissal as a last resort after other measures to get ailing firms into shape had been considered first.

"The idea is that a company does not have to become bankrupt...before it can adjust its staff levels," Antonio Gutierrez, head of the CCOO, told a news conference. "But with the condition that all other efforts have been exhausted."
A spokeswoman for employers association CEOE declined to comment on the progress of reform talks.
At present, labour regulations stipulate that fair worker dismissal can only be justified by economic, technical, organisational or productive reasons. The code is considered at best ambiguous.
The majority of contested redundancy cases in Spain's industrial tribunals rule in favour of the sacked employee at a higher cost for businesses.
"We want internal (corporate) flexibility measures to have run out before any dismissal steps are taken...sacking should be the last option that is adopted," a CCOO spokesman said.
This was not an attempt to undo the current dismissal code but rather to expand the rules which already exist, he said.
CCOO wants employers to try all options available to get the company back on track during a 12-month period prior to any redundancies.
The new measure will be presented to employers' groups next week, after being discussed with the nation's other leading union, the UGT, CCOO said.
So far negotiations between employers' groups and unions have made little headway over how to make Spain's jobs market more flexible and create more jobs.
The government has given them until March to reach a compromise, or it will step in and impose one.
Spain's unemployment rate, at 14.07 percent in January according to Labour Ministry figures, is among the highest in Europe.
But attempts to impose reform have had little success.
Changes introduced under the previous Socialist government in 1994 made it easier to hire temporary workers.
But critics say this opened up a wide gap in Spanish society, with young people often the victims of "junk contracts".
Temporary contracts can be renewed only a few times, depending on the type, before workers must be made permanent or dismissed.
Employers' demands so far have focused on the high cost and difficulty of dismissal for permanent workers, while the unions are concerned with the precariousness of job contracts.
